paras: The lynching of Joe Harrison took place at Big Timber, Gallatin County, Montana Territory, about 3 a.m. on July 7, 1882, when twenty to thirty men overpowered his guards and hanged and shot him.
Harrison was being held for a hearing on the charge of shooting Miss Flora Cutler, the Sweet Grass school teacher, who survived paralyzed.
Montana papers reported the killing with approval, and no paper in the coverage gives Harrison's race.

Flora Cutler came from Red Wing, Minnesota, in early June 1882 to take charge of the Sweet Grass school and boarded with the family of Wade Harrison, Joe Harrison's brother. Joe Harrison, recently arrived from California and a brother of Gallatin County deputy sheriff Al. Harrison, paid her attentions, and some papers reported the two had been engaged. At a Fourth of July ball and supper at Stillwater she refused to go in to supper or dance with him, and friends stopped him from throwing himself into the Yellowstone.

On the morning of July 6, according to the Billings Herald and a Big Timber correspondent, Harrison shot Miss Cutler at Wade Harrison's house, wounding her in the arm and lung. The Helena Herald's informant, the stage passenger J. F. Blaine, placed the shooting on July 5 and said bystanders knocked the revolver from his hand. Private citizens arrested him and brought him to the justice's court at Big Timber too late for examination, so a hearing was set for 9 a.m. and three citizens, W. H. Brown, Walter Ewing and Ben Howeseth, guarded him, there being no sheriff or constable nearby.

About 3 a.m. on July 7 a mob of twenty to thirty men overpowered the guards and hanged Harrison in the building where he was held, then shot him three or four times. In Blaine's version the lynchers were all masked; they put a lariat around his neck, stood him on a store box under a projecting beam of the store, kicked it away and fired a volley into him. The mob then crossed the Yellowstone at Kiger's ferry, forcing the ferryman to take them over, and passengers on the westbound coach saw the body cut down later that day.

A coroner's jury was to be empaneled before Justice R. B. Dunham at Big Timber at 9 a.m. on July 7, and the body was to go to Harrison's friends; no verdict appears in the coverage. The Helena Herald said the lynchers had separated quietly and there was no clue to their identity, and no report of an arrest was found. Meeting the stage on the Bozeman road, Al. Harrison drew a revolver to shoot himself on hearing of the hanging and was stopped by a friend.

Miss Cutler was nursed by her sister Iva, an artist from Brainerd, and Montana papers followed her condition through the summer. In late September the sisters passed through Billings on the way to Red Wing, Flora paralyzed and carried on a litter, and physicians said she would never recover the use of her limbs.

Montana weeklies carried the first and fullest accounts, drawn from the Gallatin News correspondent, the Independent and the Helena Herald, with headlines such as 'He Meets His Just Reward at a Rope's End'. The Independent's account, reprinted in Deer Lodge, closed by saying it was generally admitted locally that Harrison 'got his just deserts', and the Helena Herald wrote of 'swift justice' while calling the crowd 'merciless'. The Fort Benton River Press reprinted the Helena account under 'A Horrible Tragedy', and a Billings Herald extra described the hanging 'by Vigilantes'.

Outside Montana the story ran as a short item that drifted from the local facts. The Seattle Post-Intelligencer headed it 'A Villain Served Right' and had him hanged from a tree, the Illinois Staats-Zeitung described a 'farmer' near Bozeman shot by 'Vigilanten', and the Bismarck Tribune told of a mob tearing the roof off a house to shoot him. Minnesota papers, interested in the 'Red Wing Girl', at first reported her murdered by 'a half-crazy crank' and Harrison still in custody. None of the coverage mentions race.

Accounts differ on the date of the shooting, July 6 in the earliest local reports and July 5 in Blaine's account, and the Dillon Tribune dated the lynching the 6th. The Big Timber correspondent printed in the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner described the mob as 'unmasked', while the Independent and the Helena Herald said the men were masked. Blaine said an officer took Harrison in charge, against the correspondent's statement that only private citizens guarded him, and the Bismarck and Brainerd versions of a sheriff's posse or a jail with its roof torn off do not appear in any Montana account.

reader.title: Lynching of Joe Harrison
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Twenty to thirty men overpowered the private guards holding Harrison for trial and hanged and shot him (A2, A3, A4).

A band of twenty to thirty men took a prisoner awaiting examination from his guards and hanged and shot him for shooting Miss Cutler (A2, A4); papers described it as 'swift justice' and his 'just deserts' (A3, A4). No paper gives Harrison's race.

A Big Timber correspondent of the Gallatin News (A2), the Independent (A4) and a stage passenger's account (A3) agree that Harrison was taken from his guards and hanged and shot at Big Timber; distant papers carried divergent versions of the method (A15, A16).

accounts.label: Big Timber correspondent (Gallatin News) and Independent
accounts.gist: Harrison was arrested by private citizens and held at Big Timber for a hearing; about 3 a.m. on the 7th twenty to thirty men overpowered the guards, hanged him in the building and shot him, then crossed the river at Kiger's ferry.

accounts.label: Stage passenger J. F. Blaine (Helena Herald)
accounts.gist: An officer took Harrison to the store at Big Timber under heavy guard; masked lynchers disarmed the guards, stood him on a store box under a beam with a lariat and fired a volley into him as he hung.

accounts.label: Distant wire versions
accounts.gist: Masked men took him from a jail to a tree and hanged him (A16, A22); or a mob overtook a sheriff's posse taking him to Bozeman, tore the roof off the house where they sheltered and shot him (A15, A17).

framing.detail: Montana papers headlined 'He Meets His Just Reward at a Rope's End' and reported that locals thought he 'got his just deserts', while calling him a 'young fiend' and the crowd 'merciless'.
The Seattle Post-Intelligencer headed its item 'A Villain Served Right'.
Minnesota papers framed the story around the 'Red Wing Girl', at first wrongly reporting her murdered and Harrison in custody.
